items.question: Why do you think deep learning and symbolic reasoning need to be combined?
items.object: Combining deep learning and symbolic reasoning
items.answer: I've never been in the purely symbolic camp. Like, if you go back to my earliest writing about, “Yes, we need program synthesis,” I was saying we need deep learning guided program synthesis. We need a merger of intuition and pattern recognition, together with discrete, step-by-step reasoning and search, into one single data structure. And I've said very repeatedly for the past eight years or so that human cognition really is a mixture of intuition and reasoning, and that you're not going to get very far with only one of them. You need the continuous kind of abstraction that's provided by vector spaces, deep learning models in general, and the more discrete symbolic kind of abstraction provided by graphs and discrete search.

items.question: How do you distinguish the forms of reasoning that matter when evaluating LLMs?
items.object: Reasoning and adaptation to novelty in LLMs
items.answer: I don't really have a single definition of reasoning. I think it's a pretty loaded term, and you can mean many different things by that. But there are at least two ways in which I see the term being used, and they're actually pretty different. So, for instance, if you're just, let's say, memorizing a program and then applying that program, you could say that's a form of reasoning. Like, let's say in school you're learning the algorithm for multiplying numbers. Well, you're learning that algorithm. Then when you have a test, you're actually applying the algorithm. Is that reasoning? I think yes, that's one form of reasoning. And it's the kind of reasoning that LLMs and deep learning models in particular are very good at. You're memorizing a pattern, and at test time you're fetching the pattern and applying it. But another form of reasoning is when you're faced with something you've never seen before, and you have to recombine the cognitive building blocks, your access to your knowledge and so on, into a brand-new model and do so on the fly. That is also reasoning, but it's a very different kind of reasoning and internalizes very different kinds of capabilities. So I think the important question about deep learning models and LLMs in particular is not, “Can they reason?” There's always some sense in which they are doing reasoning. The more important question is, “Can they adapt to novelty?” Because there are many different systems that could just memorize programs provided by humans and then apply them. What's more interesting is, can they come up with their own programs, their own abstractions on the fly?

items.question: How do you envision programming from input-output pairs becoming accessible to nontechnical users?
items.object: Programming from input-output pairs
items.answer: Broadly speaking, I think programming from input-output pairs will be a widespread programming paradigm in the future, and that will be accessible to anyone because you don't need to write any code, right? You're just specifying what you want the program to do, and then the computer just programs itself. And if there's any ambiguity, by the way, in what you meant—and there will always be ambiguity, especially if the instructions are provided by a nontechnical user—well, you don't have to worry about it because the computer will ask you to clarify. It'll say, “Okay, so I created basically the most plausible program given what you told me, but there is some ambiguity here and there. So what about this input? Currently I have this output. Does that look right? Do you want to change it?” As you change it iteratively, you are creating this correct program in collaboration with the computer.

items.object: An architecture for lifelong distributed learning
items.answer: Yeah, I think we're going to need a completely new type of architecture to implement lifelong distributed learning, where you have basically many instances of the same AI solving many different problems for different people in parallel, and looking for commonalities between the problems and commonalities between the solutions. items.question: How do you think OpenAI's O1 model works?
items.object: OpenAI's O1 model
items.answer: Well, you know, we can only speculate. I'm not sure how it really works, but it seems to be running a search process in the space of possible chains of thought, trying to evaluate which branches in the tree work better, potentially backtracking and editing if the current branch is not working out. It ends up with this very long, unsophisticated, and plausibly near-optimal chain of thought, which represents basically a natural language program describing what the model should be doing. And in the process of creating this program, the model is adapting to novelty. And so I think something like O1 is a genuine breakthrough in terms of the generalization power that you can achieve with these systems. We are far beyond the classical deep learning paradigm.

items.question: How do you understand ARC Prize’s success in the context of the changing narrative around AI in 2024?
items.object: ARC Prize’s success and its role in the changing AI research narrative
items.answer: I think we learned a lot. And overall it's been a big success. I think in 2024 we've seen a huge shift in the narrative around AI. Where previously the mainstream narrative was that we could just train larger models on more data, 100x larger models or 100x more data, and get something that's basically AGI. More recently, in the past year or so, there's been this realization that actually we were going to need something akin to System 2 reasoning, that it is not something that will simply emerge from pre-training larger models on larger datasets, that you need to add it to the system somehow. And of course, you can use test-time search. You can use program synthesis. You can use these sorts of techniques to do it. And I think it was really part of that narrative shift. And it's part of the reason also why ARC has been very popular, with lots of teams entering, lots of people talking about it and using it as a kind of reference for whether we might have achieved AGI or not, which, by the way, is not what ARC is intended to be. We just intend it to be a tool, a research tool that gets you to think about the right problems, to focus on the right directions. And really, the reason why it's been successful is because there was a latent demand for something like this. Many people had this intuition that, yes, plain LMs weren't going to get to that. We needed something more there as a replacement to LMs or some kind of superstructure around them, and that we implement System 2. And there was this intuition floating around, and I think lots of people just latched onto ARC Prize as a concrete sign that their intuition was right.

items.question: What do you take away from comparing the ARC Prize tracks with very different compute budgets?
items.object: Compute efficiency across the ARC Prize competition tracks
items.answer: On the main track, people are submitting notebooks effectively that are going to have to run on a VM in less than 12 hours, and the VM has just a P100 GPU. So this is equivalent to a total of roughly ten bucks' worth of compute per submission. And then we had the public leaderboard, which was targeted at frontier models. Each submission on that leaderboard can use up to $10,000 in API credits. So that's 1,000 times more in terms of compute than the private leaderboard. And on a per-task basis, it's actually a little bit less because we're evaluating on more tasks. We're evaluating on the 400 tasks from the public eval and then 100 from the semi-private eval, which is really what we're looking at. And on a per-task basis, that's about 200 times more compute. And what was really remarkable and frankly quite shocking is that the scores you end up seeing on the public leaderboard track what you're seeing on the private leaderboard. In both cases, we're at about 55%. And this tells you that really it's not just about throwing more compute at the benchmark. Compute is really a multiplier for ideas. And of course, if you have infinite compute, you can solve the benchmark in a very stupid way, like via brute-force search, for instance. But having better ideas really gives you dramatically more leverage for your compute, right? Which is why we end up with solutions consuming ten bucks of compute that are doing like 55%, and meanwhile solutions consuming ten kilowatts of compute doing the exact same. They're just not nearly as compute-efficient.

items.question: How do you see test-time training changing a language model's ability to generalize on ARC tasks?
items.object: Test-time training for language models on ARC
items.answer: The other category of approaches has been test-time training, where you're going to be using an LM to directly try to predict the solution, given a task description. So you're looking at a set of demonstration pairs, and then you're looking at an input grid, and you're directly trying to generate the output grid, which is a process we call transduction, as opposed to induction. With program synthesis, program induction, you're trying to write down the program that will map the input to the output grids. And in transduction you're just trying to directly predict the output grid. And of course, if you try to do this with LMs and you stay within the classical deep learning paradigm, where you have this big model that's pre-trained on tons of data, and then at inference time it is static and you're really just running a forward pass of the model, you really cannot adapt to any meaningful amount of novelty, right? You are stuck memorizing patterns and, at test time, fetching and reapplying the patterns that you've memorized. To go beyond that, people have started using test-time training, which is the idea that you start by pre-training this base model that knows about ARC, knows about ARC tasks, and at inference time, on each new task that you see, you're going to try to fine-tune the base model on the demonstration pairs, to basically try to recombine the knowledge contained within latent space into a new model that is adapted to the task at hand. And if you don't do this test-time adaptation, then LLM-based transduction models are stuck below 10% accuracy, roughly. But if you start doing test-time training, then you're unlocking a dramatically higher level of generalization. And you can go well into the 50%, 55%, probably even 60% soon.

items.question: Why do you favor an approach like OpenAI’s O1 over test-time training for adapting to novel tasks?
items.object: Test-time training versus program search for adapting to novelty
items.answer: Well, I'm not sure what we do exactly. Of course we are doing active inference. What does that mean exactly? What algorithms, what data structure are we leveraging? We don't know. So I can't really tell you what's the difference. It does seem to me—I will say one thing. When you're doing test-time training with an LLM, you are letting a gradient descent process do the knowledge recombination. To adapt to novelty, it is necessary to take the knowledge that you have and recombine it in some way. And there are multiple different things you could be doing to achieve that. You could be doing program search, where the thing that is adapted to the new task is a program, and you are building this program via a search process. Something like what the O1 model from OpenAI is doing is very similar to that, where you are doing search effectively in the space of chains of thought, and you are writing down this chain of thought, which is basically a natural language program for the model to execute. And you're doing this search via a sort of AlphaZero-style tree search process. That's one take. You can also just use discrete program search to write down the program, and the program is the artifact that models the task at hand. Or you can try to modify the weights of the model, modify representations of the model to create a new model that's adapted to the task. In this case, the artifact that's adapted to the task is the model itself. And that's what test-time training does, and it does it via gradient descent. My take is I don't think humans adapt to novelty by recombining what they know via gradient descent specifically. I think the level at which we represent knowledge, especially in the context of solving ARC puzzles, is much more abstract and symbolic in nature, and the way we combine it is much closer to functional composition than it is to what you can achieve with gradient descent, right? In general, I don't think it's a good idea to try to use gradient descent as a replacement for a programming process. So I'm actually more of a fan of what a system like O1 is doing than trying to do test-time training.

items.question: How do you assess the possibility of overcoming transformers' generalization limitations through architecture changes?
items.object: Architecture changes as a way to overcome transformers' generalization limitations
items.answer: I think it's entirely plausible. As you point out, even given lots of data, there are many algorithmic tasks that you cannot train a transformer to do, or even if you can, it will learn a solution that does not generalize very well. It will work on inputs that are pretty close to what it's been trained on. If you try an input that is very far away from the training distribution, it will just fail. People will think we can move past these limitations; they're saying that we can make architecture tweaks, and they're right. It is always possible to take a deep learning model, modify the architecture to bake into it some strong structural priors about the algorithmic problem that you're trying to solve. And now you can actually use gradient descent to find a solution that will generalize, right? But the way this works is by asking a human engineer effectively to first understand the task at hand and convert that symbolic understanding into a better architecture, an architecture that is, in some important ways, isomorphic to the causal structure of the problem. Of course, if you want to autonomously adapt to novelty, you cannot just require a human engineer to intervene in writing your architecture. The process has to be fully autonomous. And so the question is, can you create an architecture search or architecture generation machine that will take a problem, identify the key elements of the problem structure that you need to bake into a new architecture, and then generate the architecture? If you can do that, then sure, maybe you can leverage that to achieve strong generalization. But I think that problem is at least as difficult as program search in the general case.

items.question: What do you think the ensemble results from the 2020 and 2024 ARC competitions reveal about the benchmark's ability to measure progress toward AGI?
items.object: ARC-1 benchmark saturation and brute-force scaling
items.answer: So in the very first ARC competition on Kaggle back in 2020, the highest score by a single submission was only 20%. That was the winner, and it was doing just basic brute-force program enumeration. But if you looked at all of the submissions in the competition and ensembled them together, you would see a high score of 49%, which would have been, until very recently, state of the art. And that was again like four years ago. And what that tells you is that about half of the private test set is easily brute-forceable, because every single entry in the competition back in 2020 was doing some kind of brute-force program enumeration. That is not AGI, that is not the sort of solution that we're looking for. And so the fact that doing this kind of stuff at scale could get you 49% is a very strong sign that the benchmark is flawed. Today, if you look at the 2024 competition, the state of the art for any single submission is about 55%. So you could say, okay, we're very far from the benchmark since the bar is 85%. And we also know that humans can solve very close to 100%. Like, if I showed you the private test set, you'd probably do 97, 98, 99%. And if you take an ensemble of everything that was submitted in the competition in 2024, you would get to a high score of 81%, which is pretty close to what we are looking for. And I don't think anything that was tried in the competition this year is really close to AGI in a meaningful sense, and the ensemble of everything is still not close to AGI. items.question: Why do you favor a three-set evaluation protocol for ARC-2?
items.object: ARC-2's three-set evaluation protocol
items.answer: It's going to be leveraging three sets. There's going to be the public eval, the semi-private eval, and the private eval. One problem with the first few competitions on Kaggle is that we've been reusing the same private test sets across every competition, and anytime anyone made a submission, they could immediately see their score on the private eval. This can actually lead to some amount of information leakage about the private test set over time. In fact, there are very well-documented techniques about how you can start to reconstruct, given enough submissions, the contents of the private eval. We want to avoid this in the competition next year. The way we're doing this is that we're going to be evaluating on the semi-private eval during the competition. So when you submit something, you get your semi-private score, and only at the very end of the competition, to create the final leaderboard, are we actually going to run the submissions on the fully private test set. Another nice thing if you do that is that this enables you to make a direct apples-to-apples comparison between the Kaggle leaderboard and the public leaderboard with all the frontier models. Of course, it's not going to be the same amount of compute, but the score is going to be apples to apples.

items.question: How do you understand why program induction and deep-learning transduction solve substantially different sets of ARC tasks?
items.object: Program induction and deep-learning transduction on ARC tasks
items.answer: That's actually one of the most interesting findings of the 2024 competition: program induction and doing transduction with deep learning models, typically an LM, lead to solving substantially different sets of tasks. This was surprising to me, but in retrospect it makes sense, especially if you start looking at the task and analyzing what makes them different. There are some tasks that are very perceptual in nature, right? They are effectively pattern-recognition problems. And this is the kind of task that you solve well with transduction methods. There are other tasks that are much more algorithmic in nature and much more discrete in nature. You cannot provide an easy solution based on pattern recognition, but it is very easy to just write down an algorithm to produce the solution. And in reverse, if you look at ARC puzzles that are very perceptual, it is very challenging to write solution programs for them, because the program would have to formalize a lot of concepts, perceptual concepts that make intuitive sense for us, but that are actually very difficult to express in program form. Imagine trying to recognize the letter A, for instance. If you're just looking at letters, you can immediately see, if you have a sort of pre-training visual knowledge of the shape of letters, this is a trivial problem. You just recognize letters. It's just what you do. It's pattern recognition. But if you try to write down an algorithm that would take a handwritten letter and tell you if it's an A, for instance, it's actually tremendously difficult.

items.question: Why do you consider Kevin Ellis and team's strategy of starting with induction and falling back on transduction a smart way to combine the two methods?
items.object: Kevin Ellis and team's strategy of starting with induction and falling back on transduction
items.answer: Well, the way Kevin Ellis and team are doing it in their paper is basically they are starting with induction and they are falling back on transduction when it doesn't work. And I think that's a very smart strategy because induction is actually formally verifiable. You can try to run your candidate program on the demonstration pairs that you have access to and see: first of all, does it run? And second, does it get you the right result? If it does, you can have a fairly high degree of confidence that it is going to generalize. Whereas when you're doing transduction, it's more like you're guessing where the answer might be, and you don't really have any way to verify that this is the right guess. One thing you can do is increase the sample size. You can make many independent guesses, and then you can look at which answers come up most often. But you're basically making the assumption that wrong guesses are all going to be wrong for different reasons, so you're going to end up with different wrong answers. Correct guesses are all going to be correct for the right reasons, so the correct answer will show up more often. But surely you have no way to make sure 100% that your guesses are correct. So it's much smarter to start with induction, because then you can have a high degree of confidence that the solution you have is the right solution, and then fall back when it just doesn't work. So basically induction is the method you should prefer.

items.question: Why do you think making a neural network learn shared representations across different views of an ARC problem helps it understand the problem better?
items.object: Learning shared neural network representations across different views of an ARC problem
items.answer: My basic intuition is that if you look at the same problem from different angles, you are more likely to come up with the true shape of the problem. And this is especially true if your data structure of choice is a neural network, because neural networks have this tendency to latch on to noisy statistical regularities. And if you're only targeting one problem and only using one input modality, you're much more likely to overfit to elements of noise within that problem. But if you are forcing the same representations to work across many different views of the problem, first of all, you get better information about the problem, right? Because there is some knowledge transfer, some information exchange between things like trying to predict the output grid and trying to generate more input grids, for instance. But also it acts as a regularization mechanism where the noise that you might be learning with one of the modalities is going to be countered with what you're learning with another modality, another approach.

items.question: What do you find compelling about Clément Bonnet and MacFarlane’s approach to test-time adaptation in latent program space?
items.object: Clément Bonnet and MacFarlane’s approach to test-time adaptation in latent program space
items.answer: This is actually personally one of my favorite papers that was submitted in the competition. It is this very original idea that you're going to be learning a latent space of programs and then at test time—you need some adaptation to the problem at hand, some recombination of your knowledge. Some people use test-time training, some people use search. What Clément Bonnet and his colleague MacFarlane are doing is very original. They're learning this latent space of programs, and then at test time they are doing gradient descent in latent program space to basically move around latent program space and find the point of the space that matches best the task. I think this is a great idea. There are many ways to improve the idea, but it's a very original take on test-time adaptation. That is not search, that is not fine-tuning. So I like it a lot.

items.question: How would you improve a system that searches for programs using gradient descent in latent program space?
items.object: Improving gradient descent-guided search in latent program space
items.answer: I think one way to improve the process is that you could also try to decode your latent programs back into a symbolic, discrete form. And then you can start doing local discrete search around the decoded programs. The benefit of that approach is that you would have the ability to actually run the programs and verify whether they work. And as long as you stay in latent space, even if you're doing this gradient descent-guided search within latent space to find the best possible points that represent a target program, you are very much limited to guessing. You have no way to assert that what the latent space is telling you matches the reality on the ground. So the ability to decode back into real program space, write and run these programs, would be a very good addition to the system.

items.question: How would you approach deep learning guided program synthesis if you spent a year working on ARC?
items.object: Deep learning guided program synthesis for ARC
items.answer: I'd be doing deep learning guided program synthesis. And I think the way people are doing deep learning guided program synthesis today is wrong. Everyone is leveraging LMs, which of course makes sense because there are these very powerful tools that contain a lot of useful knowledge that can be applied to any problem. We've invested billions and billions of dollars into creating this tool. So not using these tools would feel like you're missing out on a lot of power, but I think it is not the right approach to treat program synthesis as just token-by-token code generation. I think the right way to think about a program is as a graph of operators, and program search, program synthesis, is basically a tree-search process. I think you're better off trying to use deep learning models, and in particular LLMs, to guide that search process. This is not something that many people are trying today, but I think this would be closer to the right approach.

items.question: What do you think human ARC puzzle solving suggests about the role of descriptive models in program search?

items.answer: Another thing that people are not doing today, but should be, is that if you look at the way humans solve ARC puzzles, they are not trying many different solution programs in their mind. They are only trying a few. I think humans have the capability to first describe a model where they think and use this model, basically describing a grid in terms of the objects it contains, their properties, and their relationships with other objects, with a focus on causal relationships in particular. So you can use these descriptive models to constrain the search space when you're finally looking at input-to-output programs. items.question: How do you think about using a domain-specific language rather than Python to solve ARC tasks?

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between fuzzy pattern recognition and human System 2 reasoning?
items.object: Human System 2 reasoning as structured, iterated fuzzy pattern recognition
items.answer: I think the fundamental cognitive units in the human brain are actually fuzzy pattern recognition. That's the core thing that you do. And then when you are doing something that's more akin to reasoning or planning, when you're doing basically System 2 processing, this sort of slow, logical, step-by-step processing, what you're really doing is iteratively applying your intuition, but in a structured form. And by the way, this is exactly what deep learning guided program synthesis is about, which is the approach I've been advocating for since 2017. What are you doing when you're doing deep learning guided program synthesis? You are building a program, so basically a graph of operators, but you're building it step by step. And at each step, when you're choosing what to edit in your graph, what to add, what branching decision to make, you're applying your intuition. You're applying a guess provided by a deep learning model, right? So you're iteratively guessing to create this highly structured symbolic discrete artifact, this program. And when you're running this program, that's System 2. I think this is basically the way we do System 2 as humans: we are iteratively guessing, iteratively applying fuzzy pattern recognition to construct an artifact that is in fact symbolic in nature. Like, let's say you're playing chess. When you're calculating in your mind, you're unfolding some moves step by step, but you're only going to be doing it for a few of the moves that are on the board. And how do you select which moves to look at? You're applying pattern recognition. And then when you're simulating one move into the future, you're not going to be simulating the entire board. You're going to be focusing on some areas. So again, that's pattern recognition. And sometimes any sort of pattern recognition is basically a guess at heart. So it might be wrong, right? In some way. Sometimes in chess you're calculating and some of your intuition about future states of the board is wrong, and then you play the move and realize, “Oh, oops.” And so I think this is basically how humans implement System 2. items.question: How do you interpret the role of consciousness in turning iterated fuzzy pattern recognition into deliberate reasoning?
items.object: Consciousness as a self-consistency check on iterated pattern recognition
items.answer: This is the basis of my current favorite theory for how to interpret consciousness: in order for something like System 2 to arise from iterated fuzzy pattern recognition, that iteration sequence needs to be highly self-consistent. Everything you add, you need to double-check that it matches what came before it. If you're just iteratively pattern-matching with no guardrails whatsoever, you're basically hallucinating. You're dreaming. This is exactly what happens when you're in a dream state, by the way. You're just repeatedly intuiting what comes next, with no regard whatsoever for consistency, for self-consistency with the past. And I think this is the reason why any sort of deliberate logical processing in the brain needs to involve awareness, needs to involve consciousness. Consciousness is this sort of self-consistency check. It's the process that forces the next iteration of your intuition, of this pattern-recognition process, to be consistent with everything that came before it. And the only way to achieve this consistency is via these back-and-forth loops that are bringing the past into the present, bringing your prediction of the future into the present. So you have this nexus point in the present, this thing you're focusing on. And that nexus is basically your consciousness. So consciousness is the process that forces iterated pattern recognition to turn into something that's actually reasoning, that's actually self-consistent.

items.answer: I've never been in the purely symbolic camp. items.question: How do you distinguish the different kinds of reasoning?
items.object: Reasoning as applying memorized programs versus adapting to novel problems
items.answer: I don't really have a single definition of reasoning. I think it's a pretty loaded term, and you can mean many different things by that. But there are at least two ways in which I see the term being used, and they're actually pretty different. So, for instance, if you're just memorizing a program and then applying that program, you could say that's a form of reasoning. Like, let's say in school you're learning the algorithm for multiplying numbers. While you're learning that algorithm, then when you have a test you're actually applying the algorithm. Is that reasoning? I think yes, that's one form of reasoning. And it's the kind of reasoning that LLMs and deep learning models in particular are very good at. You're memorizing a pattern, and at test time you're fetching the pattern and reapplying it. But another form of reasoning is when you're faced with something never seen before, and you have to recombine the cognitive building blocks, your access to your knowledge and so on, into a brand-new model and do so on the fly. That is also reasoning, but it's a very different kind of reasoning, and it underlies very different kinds of capabilities.

items.question: Why do you consider adaptation to novelty a more important question about LLMs than whether they can reason?

items.answer: So I think the important question about deep learning models and LLMs in particular is not, “Can they reason?” There's always some sense in which they are doing reasoning. The more important question is, can they adapt to novelty? Because there are many different systems that could just memorize programs provided by humans and then reapply them. What's more interesting is, can they come up with their own programs, their own abstractions on the fly? And what would it mean for a system to come up with its own abstractions? items.question: Why do you think creating new AI benchmarks and developing solutions to them should go together?
items.object: Co-evolving AI benchmarks and solutions
items.answer: I think both. I'm a pretty strong believer in the idea that you need to co-evolve the solution together with the problem, and that was actually the motivation for creating ARC-1 in the first place: to have the right challenge that forces you to focus on the right questions, on the main bottlenecks to achieving strong generalization with AI. And so I don't think ARC-1 is the last benchmark. Of course there's going to be a V2 of ARC-1, but that also is not going to be the last benchmark. I think we are always going to be needing new benchmarks, exploring new things that are hard for AI and easy for humans.

items.question: Do you think working on ARC-1, a benchmark you created, amounts to cheating?
items.object: Working on ARC-1 as its creator
items.answer: I don't think so. The benchmark is meant as a tool for research. Something like ARC-1, for instance, is not really meant as a binary indicator telling you, “Oh, do we have AGI or not?” It's really meant as a research tool. It's a challenge that forces you to work on the right questions, that can direct your attention to the right problems and help you make progress. So you could say that ARC is basically a compass towards AGI. It's not like a test for AGI. And there's a spectrum of possible solutions to ARC. items.question: How do you envision programming from input-output pairs working as a widespread programming paradigm?
items.object: Programming from input-output pairs
items.answer: Broadly speaking, I think programming from input-output pairs will be a widespread programming paradigm in the future, and that will be accessible to anyone because you don't need to write any code, right? You're just specifying what you want the program to do, and then the computer just programs itself. And if there's any ambiguity in what you meant—and there will always be ambiguity, especially if the instructions are provided by a nontechnical user—well, you don't have to worry about it because the computer will ask you to clarify. It'll say, “Okay, so I created basically the most plausible program given what you told me, but there is some ambiguity here and there. So what about this input? Currently I have this output. Does that look right? Do you want to change it?” As you change it iteratively, you are creating this correct program in collaboration with the computer.

items.question: How do you envision the architecture needed to implement lifelong distributed learning in AI?
items.object: An architecture for lifelong distributed learning
items.answer: Yeah, I think we're going to need a completely new type of architecture to implement lifelong distributed learning, where you have basically many instances of the same AI solving many different problems for different people in parallel, and looking for commonalities between the problems and commonalities between the solutions. items.answer: Well, I think something like O1 is already doing precisely that. items.answer: So the difficulty in applying test-time training in actual frontier models is not so much the infrastructure. items.question: Why do you see OpenAI's O1 model as a breakthrough in generalization?
items.object: OpenAI's O1 model
items.answer: Well, you know, we can only speculate. I'm not sure how it really works, but it seems to be running a search process in the space of possible chains of thought, trying to evaluate which branches in the tree work better, potentially backtracking and editing if the current branch is not working out. It ends up with this very long, unsophisticated, and plausibly near-optimal chain of thought, which represents basically a natural language program describing what the model should be doing. And in the process of creating this program, the model is adapting to novelty. items.question: How do you understand the claim that the test-time scaling law is a new development?
items.object: The test-time scaling law
items.answer: So the test-time scaling law is basically this observation that if you expend more compute, if you search further, you see a corresponding improvement in accuracy. And that relationship is logarithmic, by the way. Accuracy improves logarithmically with compute. I don't think this is really new. Anytime you do test-time search, you will see this relationship. If you're doing brute-force program search, for instance, you will find that your ability to solve a problem improves logarithmically with the amount of compute. If you have more compute, you can just search further into the space of possible programs, and logarithmically you find more solutions. So anytime you do any kind of test-time search you will see this relationship.

items.answer: I don't use LMs all that much when I'm programming.
